question: On a 3x3 Rubik's Cube, how many non-top-facing stickers must be seen to fully identify the PLL case when solving using the CFOP method?

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: 8

After OLL the U face is a solid colour, so the top stickers carry no information about permutation. All of the PLL distinction is in the lateral stickers of the 8 U-layer pieces.

There are 4 U-layer edges, each of which contributes a single visible non-U sticker, and 4 U-layer corners, each of which contributes a single visible non-U sticker from the viewpoint you are using to read the case. One side sticker per piece is enough to tell which physical piece is sitting in that U position, because the U sticker is already known to be correct from OLL.

So in practice you have to be able to read one lateral sticker for each of the 4 edges and one lateral sticker for each of the 4 corners. That is 4 + 4 = 8 non-top-facing stickers that must be observable in order to unambiguously name the corner permutation and the edge permutation, and therefore the PLL case. With fewer than that you can have two different PLLs that are indistinguishable on the visible lateral information.

3.text:
In CFOP the OLL is done first. After an OLL the whole U face is
monochrome so the U face itself carries no permutation information at
all.  All of the information which distinguishes one PLL from another
is therefore carried by the side colours of the eight U-layer pieces.

The U-layer is

* 4 U-edges : U-sticker + 1 side sticker
* 4 U-corners : U-sticker + 2 side stickers

so that formally the U-layer is described by

4 ×1 + 4 ×2 = 12

non-U stickers.  That is the 12 side stickers of the top layer which
are the only bearers of PLL information.

In ordinary recognition you do not have to write down all twelve of
them.  The edge permutation is the permutation of the four side
colours

UF , UR , UB , UL

and the corner permutation is the permutation of the four corner
pieces up to rotation.  Up to the global rotation of the cube the
case can be recognised from the four U-edge side stickers and one
distinct side sticker per U-corner, i.e. the eight distinct side
colours of the U-layer, the four edge side stickers and the four
corner side stickers that are normally quoted as the ‘headlights’,
the ‘blocks’, etc.  This is the eight-sticker, in the literature
often seven-sticker, practical recognition set.  The twelve stickers
above are the complete formal description of the U-layer.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: After OLL the U face is monochrome and carries no permutation information. All PLL distinction is therefore in the U-layer side stickers.

* Formal inventory of the U-layer: 4 U-edges each have 1 non-U sticker and 4 U-corners each have 2 non-U stickers, i.e. 4×1+4×2 = 12 non-top-facing stickers belong to the last layer. That is the complete formal description of the layer.

* Practical identification: an U-edge is identified by its single side sticker; a U-corner is identified up to rotation by the U sticker plus its two side colours. In ordinary recognition one side sticker per cubie is enough. That is 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 distinct side colours that are normally read, the four edge side stickers E1..E4 and one side sticker per U-corner C1..C4, e.g. the “headlights / blocks” etc. Colleagues 1-3 all quote this 8-sticker practical set.

* Information-theoretic bound: because the 8 U-cubies are a permutation with parity constraint, the eighth cubie is forced once seven are known, so seven non-U stickers are information-theoretically sufficient and eight is the usual quoted practical number.

No disagreement on the 12-sticker inventory. The debate is emphasis: 12 is the total non-U stickers on the U-layer, 8 is the minimal set you actually have to read in normal CFOP recognition, with 7 being the theoretical minimum. Unresolved for the current question is whether “must be seen” is interpreted as total stickers belonging to the layer, the usual 8-sticker recognition set, or the 7-sticker information-theoretic minimum.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I agree with Colleague 2 that the operational number you have to be able to read is eight non-U stickers, four edge side stickers plus one side sticker per U-corner.

After OLL the U face is monochrome so the U stickers carry no permutation information. Identification of a PLL is identification of which of the four U-edge pieces is in each U-edge slot and which of the four U-corner pieces is in each U-corner slot.

An U-edge is completely identified by its single side sticker; the U sticker is known. So you need the four edge side stickers UF, UR, UB, UL.

A U-corner is identified by the side colours that sit next to the known U colour. In a single fixed viewpoint you can only guarantee to see one of its two side stickers. That one side colour is enough to tell you which physical corner piece is in that U position, and with OLL done the orientation of the piece is already fixed so you do not need the second side sticker for PLL recognition. Hence you need one observable side sticker for each of the four corners.

That is 4 + 4 = 8 distinct non-top-facing stickers that must be observable to name the corner permutation and the edge permutation unambiguously in the view you are using.

The 12 non-U stickers of the U-layer that Colleague 3 and Colleague 1 count are the formal complete description of the layer, four edge side stickers and eight corner side stickers. They are not all needed for recognition because the second side sticker of a corner is redundant once the first is known and the U colour is known.

The information-theoretic seven sticker bound that Colleague 1 mentions is true only if you are allowed to use the global parity of the permutation as an extra free assumption and if you are allowed to rotate the cube for free to bring hidden stickers into view. Parity tells you even vs odd, it does not tell you which specific piece occupies the eighth slot, so in a guaranteed, single-view recognition you cannot rely on it to disambiguate two different PLLs that share the same parity. In practice recognition is quoted as the eight side stickers of the U-layer, four edges and four corners, and that is the minimum you can guarantee to see.

information. All of the PLL information is carried by the U-layer side
stickers.

Formally the U-layer is

* 4 U-edges : U + 1 side
* 4 U-corners : U + 2 sides

i.e. 4+4 = 8 distinct non-top stickers of the U-layer, the four edge
side stickers and the four corner side stickers that are normally
quoted as headlights, blocks, etc.  With the parity condition on the
U-layer permutation the eighth cubie is forced once seven of them are
known, so seven non-U stickers are information-theoretically sufficient
and eight is the usual practical recognition set.  The 12 stickers
above are the total non-U inventory of the U-layer.

After OLL the U face is monochrome and gives no permutation information. A PLL is the permutation of the 4 U-edges and 4 U-corners. The U colour of each cubie is already known, so naming is done from the side information only.

* A U-edge is named by its single side sticker. The four edges are UF, UR, UB, UL in the current orientation. You cannot identify the edge permutation without seeing all four of those side stickers. That's 4 non-U stickers.

* A U-corner is named up to rotation by the known U colour together with its two side colours. With OLL done the orientation of the corner relative to U is fixed, so one identifiable side colour per corner is enough to tell you which physical corner is in that U slot. In a single fixed viewpoint you can guarantee to see only one of the two side stickers of a given corner; the other side is hidden on the back or front face. You cannot guarantee to see the hidden side without rotating the cube away from the view you are using for recognition.

That gives 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 distinct non-top-facing stickers of the U-layer that have to be observable to unambiguously name the PLL case in one view. Those are the headlights, blocks, etc. that are normally read for PLL.

The 12 sticker inventory Colleagues 1 and 3 quote, 4 edge side + 8 corner side, is the complete formal non-U inventory of the U-layer, not the minimal recognition set. The information-theoretic 7 sticker bound is an interesting counting argument: the eighth cubie is forced by the even permutation parity of the U-layer, so seven independent non-U stickers are enough to distinguish the 21 rotation classes in principle. That bound assumes you are allowed to use parity as extra knowledge and to bring hidden stickers into view by free rotation. Parity tells you even vs odd, it does not tell you which specific piece occupies the eighth slot, and it does not give you a guaranteed observation in a fixed viewpoint.

For guaranteed, single-view CFOP recognition the conventional and safe minimum is the eight side stickers of the U-layer, four edges and four corners.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: After OLL the U face is monochrome so it carries no permutation information; all PLL information is in the side stickers of the 8 U-layer cubies.

Formal inventory of the U-layer:
* 4 U-edges: U + 1 side → 4 non-U stickers
* 4 U-corners: U + 2 sides → 8 non-U stickers
Total 4+8 = 12 non-U stickers. Colleagues 1 and 3 consistently present this 12-sticker total as the complete formal description of the last layer.

Recognition / operational set:
With U colour fixed by OLL an U-edge is named by its single side sticker UF,UR,UB,UL and a U-corner is named up to rotation by the known U colour together with its two side colours. One distinct side sticker per U-cubie is enough to name which physical piece sits in which U slot.

Practical CFOP recognition is therefore quoted as
4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 observable non-U stickers of the U-layer.
This is the headlights/blocks set Colleague 2 defends as the guaranteed single-view minimum, and Colleagues 1 and 3 also give as the usual practical set.

Information-theoretic bound:
Parity of a 3×3 means the eighth cubie is forced by the permutation of the other seven. There are 21 rotation classes of PLL. Hence seven independent non-U stickers are information-theoretically sufficient to distinguish the 21 PLL classes. Colleagues 1 and 3 note the 7-sticker bound; Colleague 2 disputes its use for guaranteed single-view recognition, arguing parity only gives even/odd and does not identify which specific piece occupies the eighth slot without free rotation, and that in a fixed viewpoint you cannot rely on it to disambiguate, so 8 stickers are needed for an unambiguous guaranteed view.

Unresolved interpretation of the question:
Formal total 12 vs practical observable 8 vs information-theoretic minimum 7. Colleague 2 frames the question as “what must be seen in one fixed view” → 8. Colleagues 1 and 3 keep all three numbers: 12 = total non-U inventory, 8 = normal guaranteed recognition set, 7 = information-theoretic lower bound under parity. Round 3 repeats these positions with no convergence on which interpretation the question intends.

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: After OLL the U face is monochrome and carries no permutation information. PLL distinction is entirely in the U-layer side stickers.

Formal inventory of the U-layer is unanimous:
* 4 U-edges ×1 side = 4 non-U stickers
* 4 U-corners ×2 sides = 8 non-U stickers
Total = 12 non-U stickers belong to the last layer. That is the complete formal description of the layer.

Practical recognition:
With U colour known from OLL, a U-edge is named by its single side sticker and a U-corner is named up to rotation by U colour + its two sides. In ordinary CFOP recognition one distinct side colour per U-cubie is enough to name the piece in its slot.
Usual quoted set = 4 edge side stickers E1..E4 + one side sticker per U-corner C1..C4 = 8 distinct non-top-facing stickers that are read, e.g. headlights / blocks etc. Colleagues 1,2,3 all quote this 8-sticker practical set.

Information-theoretic bound:
Because the 8 U-cubies form a permutation with parity constraint, the eighth cubie is forced once seven are known. Colleagues 1 and 3 state seven non-U stickers are information-theoretically sufficient and eight is the normal practical number.

Operational disagreement persists:
Colleague 2 argues the parity argument is not usable for a guaranteed single-view recognition: parity tells even vs odd but does not tell which specific piece occupies the eighth slot, so in a guaranteed, single-view recognition you cannot rely on it to disambiguate two different PLLs that share the same parity. Hence the minimum you can guarantee to see is eight distinct non-U stickers, four edges + four corners. Colleague 2 also stresses that in a fixed viewpoint you can guarantee only one of the two side stickers of a given corner; the other is hidden.
Colleagues 1 and 3 maintain the seven-sticker information-theoretic sufficiency and quote eight as the conventional practical set.

No disagreement on the 12-sticker formal inventory. Debate remains on meaning of “must be seen”: 12 = total non-U stickers belonging to the U-layer; 8 = usual CFOP recognition set / guaranteed single-view minimum per Colleague 2; 7 = information-theoretic minimum per Colleagues 1 and 3. Unresolved which interpretation the question intends. Round 3 reiterated same positions with no new evidence, Colleague 2 re-emphasising guaranteed single viewpoint and that a corner’s second side is not guaranteed visible without rotation.
